4. Production of the tea was 8,657 maunds in 1966 which has been falling since 1967 and reached the rock bottom figure of 5,172 maunds in 1972.Total expenditure as per Profit and Loss Account for the year 1972, Annexure 'C' is Tk. 15,03,300.00, accordingly cost of production per pound of tea stands at Tk. 3.54 while the selling price is Tk. 3.50. The present production of 5172 maunds per year cannot be increased substantially within the next 5 years regard being had to the fact that unlike manufacturing industries, production cannot be increased overnight by additional investment as tea plants are to be pruned, manured, tended with great care with adequate rest periods and definite programme has to be followed over a number of years by which production can be gradually increased. Even assuming that production will go upto 5,500 maunds per year in near future, the Company canont per year in near future, the Company cannot earn more than Tk. 15 lacs per year, taking the selling price of tea at Tk. 3.50 per pound. So taking the annual expenditure at Tk. 15, 03,314.44 as per balance sheet for the year 1972 (Annexure 'C') the Company far from making any profit, will go on borrowing from the Bank each year for its working capital and will earn just enough, if at all, to pay for its expenses, and will perennially be unable to meet its present liabilities of Tk. 36,18,621.75 which amount will go on increasing because the said Bank charges 15% compound interest, further each year for the amount of working capital of Tk. 10-15 lacs that the Company will be obliged to borrow from the Bank will continue to add up to the Company's liabilities with 15% compound interest thereon. It may be mentioned that in the profit and oss account of 1972 Annexure (`C' shows payment of Tk. 1,24,527.71 towards Bank interest and charges and that of year, 1973 filed by Respondent No.2 shows payment of interest of Tk. 2, 04,378.59 as such, the accumulation of 15% compound interest each year for the borrowed working capital from the Bank does not appear to be convincing. The fixed assets of the company as per latest Balance sheet for the year 1972 stands at Tk. 10,30,192.92 and taking the depreciation each year into account these fixed assets cannot fetch a value more than Tk. 9,50,000.00 and that the current assets stand at Tk. 5,00,000-00. The Company has also puchased Income Tax Bonds of Tk. 22,400.00 and the cash balance stand at Tk. 1,02,820.98. The Company has shares of Tk. 21,44,500.00 in M/S W. Rahman Jute Mills Ltd. but as this Mill has been nationalised by the President's Order No. 27-of 1972, Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises Nationalisation Order, and although Article 9 thereof provides that the Government shall pay compensation in respect of shares of the Company as may be determined by it not exceeding the paid up value of such shares, this amount is not immediately available to the Company to pay its debts and as there is no knowing when the Government will pay compensation and what amount actually they would pay. It is a speculative, highly uncertain and indeterminate amount and is not immediately available to the Company to pay its debts and as such, no reliance can be placed on its for payment of liabilities. 

 c) Advancing Tk. 30,000/- to Marina Tea Estate and Tk. 5,000/- Manager, Dhamai Tea Estate, without any sanction of the Board, in the year 1971 at a time when the Company sustained a loss of Tk. 6,74,474-26. 

 e) Surreptitious and illegal manufacture by respondent No. 2 of 26,694 lbs of tea belonging to Rajnagar and Sakera Tea Estates at the Company's own factory without knowledge of the Board and without taking any step to recover the cost for the manufacture with ulterior motive for making illegal gain. 

 20. Production of tea was very much affected during the year 1971 as most of the laborers and Babus left the garden due to Pak Military Operation in the garden. Moreover, 1972-73 was very bad time for tea-growers in Bangladesh for dislocation of export of tea as more than 50% of the tea used to be exported to former West Pakistan now Pakistan, and the Government had to provide subsidy to the tea-manufacturers at the rate 50 paisa per Ib. in 1972 and at the rate 30% of the gross sale proceeds in 1973. Due to this difficulty the overdraft of the Bank could not be liquidated in the year 1971-72, but even then the Company made a total re-payment of Taka 11,17,815.00 in 1971-72. It is submitted that the position of tea industry is gradually improving with the gradual exploration of export market of Bangladesh tea and the temporary setback which the tea- industry suffered in 1971, 1972 and 1973 will be fully recovered. 

 (c) That the sum of Taka 30,000 that was advanced to Marina Tea Estate was owned by wives of two directors of this company and was by a way of temporary advance which is commonly, done, to accommodate one garden by other in case of emergency and that amount has already been repaid. As regards Taka 5,000/- advanced to the Manager, Dhamai Tea Estate, it was made for one chop cutter machine against a receipt. 

 (e) That the manufacture of 26,694 Ibs of tea belonging to two tea estates, viz. Rajnagar and Sakere Tea Estates' at the Company's own factory, was done at their request as their machinery went out of order and for which the Company has already submitted bill and steps have been taken to recover the same and it is expected to receive it shortly. These two gardens are also owned by the directors/share-holders of this company. In fact the said tea gardens are owned by Khan Bahadur Mujibur Rahman and his family members who are equally related to the petitioners and to the respondent No. 2. There was no ulterior motive of illegal gain in this matter:-

 51.  In A.I.R. 1962 Bom. 133, In re Bilasraj Juharmal, the Company was a private company whose shares were owned by 7 members who were divided into two groups and they fell in dispute, the petitioners group are not being paid dividends, that the other group consisting of majority was alleged to be conducting in a manner oppressive to the petitioners and prejudicial to the interests of the Company. The Company which was supplying electricity under the license of the Government was not in a position to continue because the Government would not renew it as the policy of the Government is that electric undertaking should be taken over by the Government, and, as such, the main object of the Company has failed. The only work that remains to be done is the distribution of the compensation money which would be frittered away by the Directors of the Company. The substratum of the Company, therefore, has gone. The court found that the Company has not been formed solely for the working of the electric license there are other objects which are independent of one another and observed: 

 "After all, the passing of an order for winding up is a matter within the 	discretion of the Court. The remedy of compulsory liquidation is obviously a drastic remedy and should be availed of only when a clear case has been made out justifying such an action. We cannot proceed to wind up the Company on assumption. If the Company is wound up today on hypothetical consideration that the compensation money will not be available to the Company for being utilised in starting new venture and if tomorrow it turns out that the compensation money is actually available for being utilised by the company, then we will be lending ourselves in a preposterous and anomalous position. It would be impossible to undo what has been done. Before taking such an irrevocable step, the Court must be 	satisfied that the assets of the Company would be completely frittered away because of the undertaking given by the share-holders of the company. I must, therefore, hold that the petitioners have failed to prove either that the substratum of the Company has gone because the undertaking in which the company was engaged for all these years has been taken over by the Government or that it is not possible for the company to start a fresh venture within the four corner of the objects adumbrated in the memorandum". (Page 144) 

 54. In A.I.R. 1932 Pun. 32 Kirpa Ram Vs. Bharat Bank Ltd. it was held that the power given under CI. (vi)  of S. 162 for winding up the company on just and equitable ground should not be exercised unless there is very strong ground for acting upon it because companies are governed by majority of their members and where there is a domestic tribunal which has power to decide upon a question, it should, if possible, be left to the domestic tribunal. (Page 133) 

 "The fact that the majority of the share-holders including an independent share-holder like the Government are against':' the winding up of the company and desire 'the Company to continue is an important circumstance which must weigh with me in deciding whether I should or should not make a compulsory winding up 	order against the company. Of course if I hold the substratum of the company is gone, this consideration would be entirely irrelevant for in such a case the majority cannot force the minority to continue the Company." (page 276) 

 57. A.I.R. 1956 S.C. 213, Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corporation Ltd. Vs. Nageshwara Rao, arose out of an application under section162 CIs (V) and (vi); Companies Act. High Court (Company Judge) found that the Vice-Chairman grossly mismanaged the affairs of the Company, and had drawn considerable amount for his personal purposes, that arrears due to the Government, for supply of electric energy was Rs. 3,10,175-3-6, that large collections had to be made, that the machinery was in a state of disrepair, that by reason of death and other causes the directorate had become greatly attenuated and "a powerful local junta was ruling the roost" and that the share-holders outside the group of the Chairman were apathetic and powerless to set matters right On these findings High Court directed winding up under section 162 (vi), just and equitable clause, which also affirmed on appeal by the Division Bench of the High Court and subsequently by the Supreme Court of India, Supreme Court observed: 

 58. In A.I.R. 1932 P.C. I, the Ripon Press and Sugar Mills and Co. Ltd. Bellary Vs, Gopal Chelli and others, the contributors alone were interested and the Company had no creditors. Privy Council held that the fact that one of the share-holders has a preponderating voice in the Company by reason of his owing or controlling a large number of shares is of itself no reason for winding up the Company and the fact dividends had not been paid regularly is no ground for winding up the Company (page 6). 

 In 26 D.L.R. 285, Rahimuddin Ahmed Vs. Bengal Waterways Ltd. and others, a single Bench of this Court, in an application under section 162 of the Companies Act filed by a share-holder, before admitting it issued notice to the respondents and some of the major creditors of the respondent company and, after ascertaining the opinion of the creditors which was against winding up, dismissed the application summarily. It was a private limited Company and its entire shareholding was owned by the two share-holders, namely the petitioner holding one-third and his brother, Respondent No. 2 holding two-thirds of the issued share capital and the Board of Directors consisting of the petitioner as Chairman and respondent No. 2 as permanent Managing Director. It was alleged that respondent No. 2 has been doing everything arbitrarily, without calling any meeting of the Board, for his personal gain at the cost of the Company, that he has mismanaged the affairs of the Company by not holding annual general meeting or that of the Board after 1969, nor 'has he kept accounts of assets and liabilities and prepared audited balance sheet and profit and loss accounts as required under Articles of Association. He has driven out the petitioner from the office of the Company. All immovable properties and assets stood mortgaged to Bangladesh Silpa Rin Sangstha for a loan of Taka 712,08 which due to nonpayment stands at Tk. 62,80,230.06 for which a notice of demand has the been served. As per Balance sheet for the year ending 14th July, 1969, the total assets of the Company stood at Taka. 57, 23, 667.58 whereas the liabilities stood at Tk. 69, 01,029.46 on 30-3-73. 

 72. Regarding unpaid dividend of Taka 90,000/- for the year 1970, Respondent No. 2 has stated in his affidavit in opposition that because of sudden set back in 1971 the declared dividend could not be paid and asserted that the payment will be made in due course. That the year 1971 was an abnormal year, there is no doubt about that. Further the fact that dividends had not been paid regularly is no ground for winding up the Company. See A.I.R. 1932 P.C. 1, The Ripon Press and Sugar Mills and Co. Ltd. Bellary Vs. V. Gopal Chetti, Supra. 

 73. Another important fact which has a great hearing in considering the assets of the Company, is the amount of Tk. 21,44,500.00 invested as shares purchased by the Company in Messrs W. Rahman Jute Mills Ltd. This Mill has been nationalised under the President Order No. 27 of 1972, Bangladesh Industrial ill Enterprises Nationalisation Order f. Petitioners case is that although Article 9 of the said Order provides that Government shall pay compensation in respect of shares of the Company as may be determined by it not exceeding the paid up value of such shares, this amount is not immediately available to the Company to pay its debts as there is no knowing when the government wile Day compensation and what amount actually they would pay. No reliance can be placed on it for payment of liabilities. 

 76. Respondent No.2, on the other hand has contended that production of tea was very much affected during 1971 as most of the laborers and Babus left the garden due to Pak Military operation in the garden. moreover the period 1972-73 was very bad time for tea growers in Bangladesh because of dislocation of export of tea, as more than 50 % of the tea used to be exported to former West Pakistan (now Pakistan), and the Government had to grant subsidy to the tea manufacturers at the rate 50 paisa per lb. in 1972 and at the rate 30% of the gross sale proceeds in 1973. These facts have not been denied by the petitioners in their affidavit in reply. Banks overdraft could not be liquidated due to this difficulty. Respondent No. 2 has submitted that position of tea industry is gradually improving with the gradual exploration of export market and the temporary setback in 1971, 1972 and 1973 will be fully recovered. 

 94. The petitioners nave alleged various acts of mismanagement on the part of respondent No. 2 which I have already detailed earlier In stating the petitioners case and the answers given by respondent No.2 have also been stated earlier in details. These allegations, if they are admitted to be correct, are at best irregularities in the management on the part of the Respondent No.2, which are subject matter of the domestic forum, namely the Board of Directors of the Company and not of the Court. The share-holders are the better Judge as to whom they would rely for management of the Company. These allegations may very well the learned Advocate for respondent has contended be made subject matter of investigation by the Registrar under section 137, sub 5(6) of the Act at the instance of the petitioner and also u/s. 138 of the Act by the Inspector appointed by the Government. However, I do not like to express any opinion on It.
